search.primaryUse: Basic regex-based search fallback (ripgrep engine), gitignore-aware, for simple single-line patterns. For advanced features, prefer ripgrep.
triggers: You have a precise single-line pattern (identifier, TODO, error string, signature fragment).
You want simple line-anchored matches without advanced ripgrep flags.
You are pairing with find_files/fuzzy_find: discover paths first, then search contents here.
avoid: Multiline patterns → ripgrep (with --multiline).
Match counting, statistics, density analysis → ripgrep (with --count).
Hidden files or dotfiles → ripgrep (with --hidden).
Conceptual / natural-language discovery → concept_search.
Structural patterns → ast_grep; security rules → semgrep.
critical: search is SECONDARY to ripgrep for content discovery.
Use ripgrep when you need: multiline, count, hidden, or advanced flags.
Prefer ripgrep for performance-sensitive operations.
Do not shell out to grep, rg, ag, or ack.

concept_search.primaryUse: BM25 relevance-ranked content search when the query is topical or fuzzy, not a fixed regex.
triggers: You have a natural-language or bag-of-words query (themes, features, "where is auth handled?").
You lack a reliable exact pattern but need the most relevant passages first.
You want ranked snippets rather than exhaustive line-by-line regex coverage.
avoid: Exact regex or literal you can write directly → search (or ripgrep for advanced modes).
Structural / AST rules → semgrep or ast_grep.
Finding files by name or path → find_files or fuzzy_find.
critical: Ranking is probabilistic — not every query term appears in every hit.
Do not substitute concept_search for precise symbol lookup when regex is feasible.
examples: After narrowing directories with find_files, run a narrower conceptual query

ripgrep.primaryUse: PRIMARY advanced ripgrep for multiline patterns, match counting, hidden file scanning, and performance-critical operations. Use ripgrep when you need advanced flags beyond basic regex.
triggers: You need multiline patterns (config files, templates, multi-statement code blocks).
You need match counts per file or files-with-matches listing (statistics, frequency analysis).
You need to scan hidden paths or bypass .gitignore (dotfiles, configuration discovery).
You need performance optimization (timeouts, column limits, fixed strings).
You're analyzing pattern density or match statistics across files.
avoid: Simple single-line searches on default paths → use search for basic regex.
Semantic / AST structure → semgrep or ast_grep.
Path discovery by name → find_files; fuzzy filename matching → fuzzy_find.
critical: PREFER ripgrep for anything beyond basic regex searching.
ripgrep is now PRIORITIZED over 'search' for advanced features (multiline, count, hidden).
Ripgrep is the power tool for performance-sensitive operations.
Combining unsafe flags (noIgnore + hidden) can surface secrets; minimize scope.

find_files.primaryUse: Fast fd-backed discovery of paths by name fragment, extension, type, or glob — respects .gitignore by default.
triggers: You know filename, extension, or glob criteria ("all *.test.ts", "Dockerfile")
You need deterministic path lists without scoring or fuzzy typo tolerance.
You want breadth-first enumeration (empty pattern can list reachable files).
avoid: Approximate / mistyped filenames → fuzzy_find.
Searching inside file bodies → search or concept_search.
Rich repo topology + metadata stitching → ls_enhanced.
Clone / duplication analysis → find_duplicates.
critical: find_files answers "which paths" — never substitute it for grep-style content tasks.
Pair with search: narrow files here, grep contents there.
examples: Empty pattern to inventory before filtering in-agent

fuzzy_find.primaryUse: Fuzzy path matching (fzf) for approximate filenames or shuffled path fragments — returns paths, not content.
triggers: You remember part of a path or non-contiguous tokens ("auth mid" → src/auth/middleware.ts).
Typos or uncertain spelling of file or directory names.
You need quick interactive-style ranking over file paths.
avoid: Exact glob or extension filters you can express cleanly → find_files.
Content search → search or concept_search.
Repository structure maps with sizes/git hints → ls_enhanced.
critical: Results are paths only — follow with search for text inside files.
Query tokens may appear in any order; not a regex.
examples: "user repo" when the path string is half-remembered
"config prod" to surface likely env files
Then run search on chosen paths

semgrep.primaryUse: Semgrep static analysis — AST-aware rules for bugs, security, and policy checks beyond regex.
triggers: You need security / SAST-style checks or team rule packs (config mode).
You match language structure (control flow, dangerous APIs) that regex would miss or over-match.
You want rule-driven guidance with semgrep's pattern language.
avoid: Plain text or trivial literals → search.
Metavariable refactoring / rewriter workflows → ast_grep.
Concept exploration without rules → concept_search.
Duplicate-block detection → find_duplicates.
Line counts → count_lines.
critical: When semgrep reports findings, corroborate with search on call sites if needed.
Prefer semgrep over regex whenever language semantics matter for vulnerability classes.
examples: Insecure hashing / TLS patterns via registry rules
Banned API usage with autofix disabled for review
Combining pattern mode for one-off audits

ast_grep.primaryUse: ast-grep structural search and rewriting with metavariables ($VAR) for code shape discovery and safe refactors.
triggers: You capture arguments, arity, call shapes, or class members structurally.
You plan repeated refactors (rewrite) with previews.
You need AST-accurate matches where regex brittleness is high.
avoid: Team security/regression packs → semgrep.
Literal-only quick grep → search.
Copy-paste clones → find_duplicates.
Conceptual prose search → concept_search.
Path discovery → find_files / fuzzy_find.
critical: semgrep optimizes for policy/security signals; ast_grep optimizes for structural edit/search loops.
Specify language (`-l`) when required for correct trees; verify before bulk rewrite.
examples: Find all calls to deprecatedHelper(...) with $$$ARGS
Pair with search to validate edge strings after structural pass

count_lines.primaryUse: Tokei-based statistics: code / comment / blank breakdowns and language totals ("cloc but faster").
triggers: You need LOC, language mix, or comment ratios for a path or repo.
You want per-file listing using files: true or language filters via types.
You exclude vendor trees with exclude lists.
avoid: Finding text inside files → search / concept_search.
Listing paths by pattern → find_files / fuzzy_find.
Structural rules → semgrep / ast_grep.
Duplicate detection → find_duplicates.
critical: count_lines measures volume present — it does not search for features or symbols.
Use parameters (files, types, exclude) to keep output token-safe on large repos.

find_duplicates.primaryUse: jscpd clone detection — exact and near-duplicate blocks for refactors and deduplication planning.
triggers: You suspect copy-paste maintenance drag or redundant modules.
You tune minLines / mode (strict vs mild) for snippet size.
You filter languages or skip generated/test trees with ignore.
avoid: Single-pattern text search → search.
Security rules → semgrep.
Shape-based refactors of one pattern → ast_grep.
Line totals → count_lines.
critical: Follow findings with ast_grep or search to plan merges; jscpd flags similarity, not intent.
Default minLines ignores tiny noise — lower only when justified.
examples: mode: mild across shared utility folders
ignore vendor and fixtures before reporting

read_enhanced.primaryUse: Structure-aware reading: code skeletons, data slicing, highlighted excerpts — optimized for token efficiency.
triggers: Large source where you need signatures or structure instead of full paste.
JSON/YAML/TOML/CSV where jq/yq queries pull a subtree without dumping the file.
You want bat-style highlighting when available.
avoid: Tiny files where verbatim full content is simpler → builtin read.
Writing or mutating content → write_enhanced / edit_enhanced.
critical: Read the fallbacks line in output — ast-grep/jq/yq/bat may be absent.
Pass jqQuery / yqQuery to avoid shipping entire large configs to the model.
examples: yqQuery for one key in a large YAML manifest
TypeScript file for outline-level context before edit_enhanced

write_enhanced.primaryUse: Atomic, backup-friendly whole-file writes with optional streaming for large payloads (Bun-native path).
triggers: You replace entire files where atomic rename prevents torn writes.
You need optional .bak snapshots before risky changes.
You stream large content to temp then rename for safety.
avoid: Small scratch files without durability needs → builtin write.
Surgical in-file edits → edit_enhanced (code) or patch flow.
critical: Choose atomic false only when you accept direct writes; understand append + atomic read-merge costs.
Enable backup for destructive refactors; capture returned backup path when present.
examples: Regenerate generated file with atomic: true, backup: true
Large asset with streaming then rename
mode: append with atomic: true for concurrent-reader safety (mind size cost)

edit_enhanced.primaryUse: AST-aware edits via ast-grep rewrite with preview and backups; falls back to literal replace for non-code.
triggers: Refactors expressed as metavariable-safe patterns and replacements.
You need preview: true before touching disk on risky transforms.
You want backups (default on) around structural edits.
avoid: One-line typo with known exact snippet → builtin edit.
Whole-file replacement → write_enhanced.
Policy/security scanning → semgrep.
critical: preview first on dangerous changes; treat syntax_ok: false as blocking until fixed.
scope narrows are forward-compatible — heed warnings if behavior is still whole-file.
Without ast-grep, metavariable patterns will not run — only literal paths work.
examples: preview: true rename of helper($X) → newHelper($X)

shell_enhanced.primaryUse: Structured shell via Nushell JSON pipelines with Bun/POSIX fallbacks — machine-shaped output for agents.
triggers: Commands like ls, ps, git log/status, $env where JSON rows beat free text.
You want enforceJson: true (default) when Nu is available.
avoid: Interactive TUIs or opaque scripts → builtin shell/bash.
When you already have clean JSON from a dedicated tool, do not re-wrap unnecessarily.
critical: Respect cancellation: AbortSignal merges across Nu/bash/Bun.$ tiers per implementation.
Use enforceJson: false when POSIX verbatim output is required.
Tune fallbackToBun when Bun shell must be skipped.
examples: ls with sortable columns for agents
Nu absent → bash fallback with enforceJson: false

ls_enhanced.primaryUse: Repository topology: hierarchical trees, sizes, optional git hints, JSON-friendly maps (broot + native fallback).
triggers: You need nested structure, role hints, or filters (type/size) for orientation.
You want broot output when available; deterministic scans when preferBroot: false.
avoid: Flat exhaustive path lists by pattern → find_files.
Fuzzy partial path recall → fuzzy_find.
Shell-level json for one command → shell_enhanced.
critical: Cap depth and filterTypes on huge repos to control payload size before truncation.
preferBroot: false if broot misbehaves in CI or hangs.
examples: Git metadata on for change awareness
